summaries.summary: Micropost event detection uses weak supervision with positive labels, unlabeled examples, keyword filtering, and expectation regularization, but faces two key problems.
Estimating the expectation associated with a keyword is challenging even for domain experts due to unpredictable events and changing posting frequency.
Event detection performance depends on keyword informativeness, and no principled method exists for discovering new keywords and improving performance.
A human-AI loop uses crowd workers, model-crowd disagreement, and a unified probabilistic model to discover keywords, estimate expectations, and train models.
The authors claim to be the first to propose a human-AI loop approach that iteratively improves event detection models.
One contribution is a novel human-AI loop approach for micropost event detection that jointly discovers informative keywords and estimates their expectation.
One contribution is a unified probabilistic model that infers keyword expectation and simultaneously performs model training.
An extensive empirical evaluation on multiple real-world datasets shows the approach improves the state of the art by an average of 24.3% AUC.
The paper presents the human-AI loop approach, probabilistic model, experimental setup and results, related work, and conclusion in subsequent sections.
The goal is to extract informative keywords and estimate expectations using two crowdsourcing tasks and a unified probabilistic model for training.
The approach collects unlabeled microposts $\mathcal {U}$ and positively labeled microposts $\mathcal {L}$, trains $p_\theta (y|x)$, and iterates from keyword $w^{(t)}$.
Micropost classification asks crowd workers to label selected microposts as event-related or non event-related using instructions and examples.
An example micropost reports that Equifax says 143m Americans' social security numbers were exposed in hack.
The Equifax micropost describes a cyber attack event instance and is an event-instance related positive example.
An example micropost says companies need to step their cyber security up.
The cyber security micropost is general event-category related, not event-instance related, and should be considered a negative example.
Each selected micropost is labeled by multiple crowd workers, and annotations are passed to the probabilistic model for expectation inference and training.
The probabilistic model takes crowd labels and the previous model as input, producing keyword-specific expectation $e^{(t)}$ and improved model $p_{\theta ^{(t)}}(y|x)$.
Keyword discovery applies $p_{\theta ^{(t)}}(y|x)$ to $\mathcal {U}$ and calculates disagreement between predictions and $e^{(t)}$ for microposts containing $w^{(t)}$.
Microposts with the highest disagreement are selected for keyword discovery because they may explain disagreement and provide information different from existing keywords.
The expectation for `hack' is 0.20, meaning 20% of initially retrieved microposts are event-related, while a highest-disagreement micropost has $99.9\%$ predicted likelihood.
An example selected micropost reports Hong Kong securities brokers hit by cyber attacks, may face more: regulator #cyber #security #hacking https://t.co/rC1s9CB.
The example micropost contains `securities', `hit', and `attack', which better indicate relevance to a cyber security event than `hack'.
When $e^{(t)}$ is high, selected microposts contain keywords indicating irrelevance, which also help the model identify irrelevant microposts.
Crowd workers identify correct-prediction microposts and keywords indicating predicted classes; the most frequent keyword initializes the next iteration, with top-$N$ keywords requiring $N$ tasks.
This section introduces the probabilistic model that infers keyword expectation and trains the target model simultaneously, then describes model learning.

At iteration $t$, $\mathcal {U}^{(t)}$, $\mathcal {M}^{(t)}= \lbrace x_{m}\rbrace _{m=1}^M$, $N$ workers, and annotation matrix $\mathbf {A}\in \mathbb {R}^{M\times N}$ support inferring $e^{(t)}$, learning $\theta ^{(t)}$, and modeling worker reliability $\pi ^{(n)}$.
Expectation regularization is introduced for weakly supervised learning of $p_{\theta ^{(t)}}(y|x)$, with an objective covering $\mathcal {L}$ and $\mathcal {U}$.
The labeled-micropost part of the objective aims at maximizing the likelihood of the labeled microposts.
The model assumes $\theta $ is generated from a prior distribution parameterized by $\sigma $, such as Laplacian or Gaussian.
Existing keyword expectations {($w^{(1)}$, $e^{(1)}$), ..., ($w^{(t-1)}$, $e^{(t-1)}$), ($w^{(t)}$, $e^{(t)}$)} regularize training, with $e^{(t)}$ inferred.
The model's expectation for each keyword $w^{(k)}$ is the empirical expectation of posterior predictions on $\mathcal {U}^{(k)}$ containing $w^{(k)}$.
Expectation regularization uses $D_{KL}[\cdot \Vert \cdot ]$ between $Ber(e^{(k)})$ and $Ber(\mathbb {E}_{x\sim \mathcal {U}^{(k)}}(y))$, with $\lambda $ controlling strength.
To learn $e^{(t)}$ and $\pi ^{(n)}$, the likelihood of $\mathbf {A}$ is modeled with expectation as class prior, connecting expectation inference with model training.
The likelihood of an arbitrary crowd-contributed label $\mathbf {A}_{mn}$ is modeled as a mixture of multinomials with prior $e^{(t)}$.
Here $e_s^{(t)}$ is the ground truth probability given the class prior, $K$ is possible ground truth labels, and $r=\mathbf {A}_{mn}$ is the crowd label.
The objective function maximizes the likelihood of the entire annotation matrix $\mathbf {A}$.
Integrating model training with expectation inference yields the overall objective function of the proposed model.
Figure FIGREF18 depicts the model combining the target model with the generative model for crowd-contributed labels through a keyword-specific expectation.
Expectation maximization handles unknown $y_m$: the E-step infers ground truth labels, while the M-step updates $\pi ^{(n)}$, $e^{(t)}$, and $\theta ^{(t)}$.
The target model parameter is updated by gradient descent, using back-propagation with gradient descent for deep neural network weight matrices.
This section presents the experimental setup and results for evaluating the approach, aiming to answer four questions.
The paragraph contains the list formatting marker [noitemsep,leftmargin=*].
Q1 asks how effectively the proposed human-AI loop approach enhances state-of-the-art machine learning models for event detection.
Q2 asks how well the keyword discovery method works compared to existing keyword expansion methods.
Q3 asks how effective crowdsourcing is at obtaining new keywords compared with labelling microposts for model training under the same cost.
Q4 asks how much benefit the unified probabilistic model brings compared to methods that do not take crowd reliability into account.
Experiments use CyberAttack and PoliticianDeath, with 11 and 8 seed events, `hack' and politician/death keywords, and 500 randomly selected tweets per dataset for evaluation.
Logistic Regression (LR) and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) are target models compared against weakly supervised methods using one initial keyword and an individual expert expectation.
Parameters use a held-out validation set with 20% of test data, MLP with 1, 2 and 3 hidden layers, grid search in 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, $\lambda =10 \times $ #labeled examples, and Adam BIBREF22.
Evaluation uses accuracy and area under the precision-recall curve (AUC), with 20% positive microposts in CyberAttack and 27% in PoliticianDeath.
Level 3 workers on Figure-Eight were used, with 50 tweets for keyword discovery and 50 tweets for micropost classification per keyword per iteration.
Table TABREF26 reports evaluation on CyberAttack and PoliticianDeath, with each iteration starting with 1 new keyword discovered in the previous iteration.
The approach improves LR by 5.17% Accuracy and 18.38% AUC, and MLP by 10.71% Accuracy and 30.27% AUC on average, with convergence between the 7th and 9th iteration by AUC.
Figure FIGREF31 evaluates informative keyword discovery against QE using pre-trained word embeddings based on a large Google News dataset and crowd-labeled tweets.
The approach outperforms QE by 4.62% and 52.58% AUC on CyberAttack and PoliticianDeath, respectively, by identifying task-related keywords beyond synonyms.
At the same cost, additional micropost labeling increases AUC by 0.87% for CyberAttack and 1.06% for PoliticianDeath, while the proposed approach increases AUC by 33.42% and 15.23%.
Figure FIGREF36 compares expectation inference with majority voting, showing improvements of 0.4% and 1.19% AUC on CyberAttack and PoliticianDeath, respectively.
The work is domain-specific event detection related to weakly supervised learning methods, contrasting with fully-supervised methods limited by training data size.
The work extends weakly supervised learning by using crowd workers to label sampled microposts for keyword-specific expectations and directly soliciting informative keywords.
The paper presents a human-AI loop approach for keyword discovery and expectation estimation that significantly outperforms the state of the art on real-world datasets.
The project received funding from the Swiss National Science Foundation grant #407540_167320 Tighten-it-All and ERC grant agreement 683253/GraphInt.
